I recently came across this vintage celery vase at a flea market in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and although I wasn’t quite sure what it was at first, I brought it home. I looked it up, of course, and I enjoyed learning about the significance of this peculiar little piece just as much as I enjoyed styling it in my space. That got me thinking: How many other once-common tablescape features have been lost to time? Apartment Therapy announced the return of the egg cup about a year ago, but what’s next?

I was sure that there must be more underrated antique pieces like this that I was missing out on, and with holiday hosting on the horizon I wanted to know what to keep an eye out for on my next thrifting trip. My father-in-law told me about a few of the items he remembered seeing on the table when he was growing up: corn cob holders, asparagus tongs, fish knives, and knife rests, all of which used to be far more common than they are today. There used to be specific serving utensils for almost every item on the table. And what all these pieces had in common was that they didn’t just serve a purpose — they were also beautiful.
Your Tablescape Can Be Both Beautiful and Functional

Of course, we all want our holiday tables to look beautiful, festive, and inviting, but visual appeal should not be the only requirement for a standout tablescape — especially not in a smaller space with limited storage and table space. So I went to the flea market to find some of those special old pieces that can do both. Read on for my guide to the vintage servingware gems you should look for on your next trip to the thrift store.

Knife and fork rests apparently date as far back as the 17th century. The metal or extra-fancy glass pieces were designed to hold utensils and prevent them from being placed directly on the table. Although the etiquette of it all isn’t so important anymore, I still think we should bring these back — after all, they’re gorgeous. And who wants stained linens?

Nothing says elegance quite like vintage flutes, and to take things a step further, go for a set that comes with a matching carafe. I can’t wait to use this blue floral set I picked up for my own table. Mix up a batch of cocktails or fruit-infused water for the table, and it’ll be a highlight for all of your guests.

Tongs were also much more commonly used in the past. Whether for asparagus or olives, they’re a far more effective way to place food on your plate than your average fork or serving spoon. And depending on the pair you find, the ornate design is sure to be a conversation starter. Don’t let your next charcuterie board or crudité platter go without this helpful vintage serving utensil.

Serving ice before freezers existed was a definitive signal of wealth. Keeping ice on hand wasn’t easy, and small ice buckets like the one I found above were a stylish way to serve it. While having to refill them isn’t the most practical, I like that the size doesn’t overwhelm the table and they’re much easier to pass around when you want to refresh your drink.

As I said above, egg cups for soft-boiled eggs are making their way back onto tables (and shelves) everywhere. If you’re having people over for breakfast or brunch, skip the scrambling and impress with this preparation instead. Bonus points if you can snag a matching spoon for eating the egg.

Special occasions often call for seafood, and seafood often calls for specialty silverware. Take time to sift through that bin of utensils and see if you can find an ornate old fish knife and fork set, or some 20th-century oyster forks. These can also easily be repurposed for a much easier-to-execute shrimp cocktail.

Way back when, dessert was the star of the show. End the meal on a high note with antique finds like a rare sugar sifter spoon or some delicate ice cream spoons. These might just be the finishing touch your table has been missing.
